name: The Cobra Effect
statement: A reward for solving a problem can make people manufacture the problem.
meaning: The cobra effect is a memorable name for a perverse incentive: an attempted solution to a problem makes it worse, because people respond to the incentive in ways the designer did not intend. The reward targets a proxy for the goal rather than the goal itself, so people optimise the proxy — even by actions that run directly counter to the original aim.
mechanism: Pin an incentive to a proxy — dead cobras, severed rat tails — that stands in for the true goal of fewer live pests, and the proxy can often be produced more cheaply by means that do not serve the goal: breeding, smuggling, or clipping-and-releasing. Rational agents optimise the proxy, and the link between proxy and goal breaks. It is the incentive-side face of Goodhart's law, that a measure made a target ceases to be a good measure, and the concrete story form of the same dynamic behind Campbell's law.

examples.text: The eponymous tale has colonial Delhi paying a bounty for dead cobras; people bred cobras for the reward, and when the scheme was scrapped released them, leaving more cobras than before — though the historical documentation of this specific event is thin and likely apocryphal.

A far better-documented case: French colonial Hanoi paid a bounty per rat tail in 1902; people cut off tails and released the rats to breed, and some ran rat farms, so the rat population and plague risk rose.
Any reward paid for a token of success — a tail, a fixed bug, a destroyed crop — rather than success itself invites the same gaming, the token manufactured to collect the reward.

variants.name: Goodhart's law
variants.text: The generalised statement that when a measure becomes a target it ceases to be a good measure; the cobra effect is its vivid, concrete illustration.

variants.name: The Great Hanoi Rat Massacre
variants.text: The documented anchor case, researched by the historian Michael Vann from colonial archives, that shows the perverse-incentive dynamic playing out in reality.

whyItMatters: It is the most memorable illustration of perverse incentives, a warning that rewarding a proxy invites people to game it, sometimes to the point of worsening the very problem the reward was meant to solve. It sharpens the design of bounties, targets, and metrics across policy and management, and it names in vivid form a genuine and well-attested phenomenon.

working.lead: Reward the goal, not the proxy
working.text: design incentives around the true outcome rather than a token that can be manufactured, to avoid gaming.
before offering a bounty or target, ask how a clever agent could collect it without serving the underlying aim.
cite the well-attested Hanoi rats rather than the shaky cobra story when illustrating the phenomenon.

limits: The specific cobra anecdote is poorly documented and likely apocryphal: its primary-source trail is a single hedged 1873 newspaper item, and an 1887 official inquiry judged deliberate cobra breeding highly improbable. The general phenomenon of perverse incentives, by contrast, is real and well-attested, the Hanoi rat case being solidly documented from the archives. The cobra effect is a coined, memorable label, not a rigorous law, and some secondary examples circulate mainly through popular retelling.
misreadings: The Delhi cobra story is not documented history — no contemporary record of cobra breeding for bounty has surfaced, and it is best labelled apocryphal. Siebert did not discover or witness the event; he coined the term in 2001 and retold an old, unverified anecdote. And the cobra effect is not a proven economic law but a heuristic and a vivid name, whose formal cousins are Goodhart's and Campbell's laws.
origin: Named and coined by the German economist Horst Siebert in his 2001 book 'Der Kobra-Effekt,' which retold the colonial-India anecdote; the well-documented parallel is the 1902 Hanoi rat-bounty episode researched by Michael Vann.
